nameStory: This climbing vine earned its name 'autumn clematis' because it puts on its most spectacular show in late summer and fall, when masses of tiny white flowers cover the plant like a snowy blanket. The sweet fragrance that wafts from these blooms gave it another common name - 'sweet autumn clematis' - making it unmistakable when you catch that honey-like scent on a warm September breeze.
description: Autumn clematis is a vigorous climbing vine that can scramble up trees, fences, and buildings to heights of 20-30 feet using its twisting leaf stems like tiny hands to grab onto supports. In late summer, it transforms into a cloud of small, creamy-white flowers that smell sweetly of honey. Originally from Asia, this ornamental escape has made itself at home throughout much of New England, though it can be quite aggressive in spreading.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Masses of small, four-petaled white flowers bloom in late summer, each about half an inch across with a sweet, honey-like fragrance that can be detected from several feet away

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with three leaflets arranged opposite each other on the stem, each leaflet oval-shaped with smooth or slightly toothed edges and a glossy green surface

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Vigorous climbing vine that uses its leaf stems (petioles) as tendrils, twisting around supports to climb high into trees or over structures

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Fluffy, silvery-white seed heads appear after flowering, creating wispy plumes that persist into winter and catch the light beautifully

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Woody stems that become quite thick with age, with opposite branching pattern and smooth bark that may develop shallow grooves on older vines

habitat: You'll find autumn clematis climbing over fences, abandoned buildings, and forest edges throughout New England, especially in disturbed areas and along roadsides. It thrives in both sun and partial shade, tolerating a wide range of soil conditions from rich garden soil to poor, rocky ground. Look for it scrambling up trees at woodland borders or completely covering old stone walls in rural areas.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as bright green compound leaflets, and the vine begins its rapid climbing growth for the season.
seasonality.summer: The vine reaches its full leafy glory and begins producing flower buds in late summer, preparing for its spectacular autumn show.
seasonality.fall: Peak blooming time with masses of fragrant white flowers covering the vine, followed by the development of silky seed plumes that persist as flowers fade.
seasonality.winter: Leaves drop to reveal woody stems and persistent fluffy seed heads that catch snow and remain visible as silvery tufts against the bare vine structure.

funFact: This sweet-smelling beauty is actually a master of deception - while its flowers smell like honey to attract pollinators, the plant is working overtime to take over native ecosystems, and a single vine can produce over 100,000 seeds in one season that can travel for miles on the wind.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with our native virgin's-bower clematis, but autumn clematis has three leaflets per leaf (not five to seven like virgin's-bower) and blooms much later in the season. Memory trick: 'Autumn has three months, autumn clematis has three leaflets.'
contextualKnowledge: Though beautiful and fragrant, autumn clematis is considered an invasive species that can smother native plants and trees. Many gardeners who originally planted it as an ornamental now struggle to control its aggressive spread, as it can quickly escape cultivation and dominate natural areas.
compareHints: Unlike our native virgin's-bower which has 5-7 leaflets per compound leaf and blooms in midsummer, autumn clematis has only 3 leaflets and saves its flowering show for late summer and fall. Purple clematis, found in northern New England, has simple (not compound) leaves and large purple bell-shaped flowers rather than masses of tiny white ones.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Virgin's-bower differs from the introduced autumn clematis by blooming later and having native range, while purple clematis has large purple flowers and grows in cooler, more northern locations.

Purple clematis stands out from its relatives by having the showiest flowers of any native New England clematis - much larger and more colorful than virgin's-bower's tiny white clusters or autumn clematis's small white stars.
